To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
timolol increases beta‐adrenergic receptors in the left ventricle and right atrium of cats with acute myocardial infarction.
chronic timolol treatment in cats increases beta‐receptor binding in the myocardium and decreases the incidence of ventricular arrhythmias and death after coronary occlusion.
timolol increased myocardial beta‐receptor number, decreased heart rate, and did not prevent post‐ganglionic cardiac nerve discharge associated with coronary occlusion‐ induced arrhythmia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of timolol on the myocardium and the sympathetic nervous system after acute coronary occlusions.
the effect of timolol on cardiac sympathetic neural activity and beta‐receptors in the heart of cats with coronary occlusion.
the effect of chronic timolol in the cat model of acute coronary occlusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
timolol may have a beneficial effect in this model for myocardial infarction.
the effect of chronic timolol on cardiac sympathetic nerve function is complex and not fully understood.
timolol may have beneficial effects in patients who have had myocardial infarction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
timolol may be beneficial to treat patients with coronary disease.
timolol, a beta‐adrenergic antagonist, has a direct effect on beta‐adrengeric receptors in the heart.
chronic timolol treatment increases beta‐receptor densities in the left ventricle and decreases the frequency of cardiac sympathetic neural discharge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
timolol is not only a beta‐adrenergic antagonist but also a neuroprotectant.
timolol may increase cardiac beta‐receptor sensitivity, which could be protective against arrhythmia.
chronic timolol treatment may increase beta‐adrenergic receptor density and decrease sympathetic neural discharge.
